#### Purpose of this file  

This file contains all of the code for producing a curated OTU table from the 16S microbial sequence data for the Armstrong et al. manuscript entitled **"XXX"**, published by [XXX](https://doi.org/10.1093/femsec/fiaa02-AAC-9).

# 4 - Plot Rarefaction Curves

## 4.1 - Prepare Metadata
```{r prep-metadata}
# Make a metadata object
metadata_df <- 
  physeq_noControlsChlorosMitos %>%
  sample_data() %>%
  data.frame()
# take a look
glimpse(metadata_df)

# Create Color dataframe for plotting 
color_df <- 
  iNEXT_input_df %>%
  colnames() %>%
  data.frame()
glimpse(color_df)

# Add a names column 
colnames(color_df)[1] <- "SampleID"
color_df <- 
  color_df %>%
  # fix sample names 
  mutate(SampleID = gsub(SampleID, pattern = "[.]", replace = "-"),
         SampleID = gsub(SampleID, pattern = "X", replace = ""))
head(color_df)

# Manual define colors
colors_subtype <- data.frame(
  "Subtype" = unique(sample_data(physeq_noControlsChlorosMitos)$Subtype),
  "Subtype_Color" = c("tomato2",
                      "tomato4",
                      "turquoise",
                      "turquoise4",
                      "goldenrod4")
  )

iNEXT_color_df <- 
  color_df %>%
  # # fix sample names 
  # mutate(names = gsub(names, pattern = "[.]", replace = "-"),
  #        names = gsub(names, pattern = "X", replace = ""))  %>%
  # Merge with metadata 
  left_join(metadata_df, by = "SampleID")

iNEXT_color_df$Subtype_Color <-
```

## 4.2 - Plot the Rarefaction Curves
```{r plot-rarefaction}
plot_rarefaction_iNEXT <- ggiNEXT(iNEXT_data, type = 1, facet.var = "Order.q") + 
  # scale_color_manual(values = iNEXT_color_df$salinity_colors) +
  # scale_fill_manual(values = iNEXT_color_df$salinity_colors) + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  labs(y = "Effective Number of ASVs",
       x = "Number of Sequences")

print(plot_rarefaction_iNEXT)

# PATCH 2026-10-26: write the figure to Figures/04-AAC-DiversityAnalyses/
ggsave(paste0(dir_out_fig, pref_out, "plot_RarefactionCurves.png"),
       plot = plot_rarefaction_iNEXT, width = 9, height = 4, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
ggsave(paste0(dir_out_fig, pref_out, "plot_RarefactionCurves.pdf"),
       plot = plot_rarefaction_iNEXT, width = 9, height = 4, bg = "white")
```

Remembering that an Order q of:  

  - 0 = Richness/ Number of Total taxa
  - 1 = Exponential Shannon / Number of "Common" taxa
  - 2 = Inverse Simpson / Number of "Dominant" taxa 
  
*Also note that iNEXT will extrapolate the number of sequences to double the sequencing depth of the sample!*

Finally, let's draw some conclusions from the plot above (we discussed in class & I'll summarize here):  

1. The best gift of a the Hill Numbers: *All three diversity measures are on the same x-axis: The Effective Number of Species or ASVs.*  
2. The y-axis values go down as we weight abundance from `q = 0, 1, 2`. As q increases from 0 to 1 to 2, the abundance of the species is weighted more, so the rarefaction curve plateaus earlier. **This is important because it indicates that richess is the most sensitive to sequencing depth!**
3. Most of the sample rarefaction curves appear to plateau but we need to look deeper.  
4. There appears to be a sample with much lower richness than the rest of the dataset. Let's keep our eyes on this sample...  

Ok, this plot is nice, but since it's autogenerated with the `ggiNEXT` function, I'd like some more freedom to plot. Let's manually plot the data that we pull out from the iNEXT data.

# 5 - Manually plot Diversity 

## 5.1 - Rarefaction
```{r iNEXT-manual, fig.width=6, fig.height=6}
iNEXT_manual_df <- 
  iNEXT_data$iNextEst$size_based %>%
  dplyr::rename(SampleID = Assemblage) %>%
  # Fix the samples names 
  mutate(SampleID = gsub(SampleID, pattern = "[.]", replace = "-"),
         SampleID = gsub(SampleID, pattern = "X", replace = "")) %>%
  # join with metadata 
  left_join(., metadata_df, by = "SampleID")

# Inspect 
dim(iNEXT_manual_df)
str(iNEXT_manual_df)

# Plot it - Rarefaction Curve 
iNEXT_manual_df %>%
  # Filter out rows that are calcaulted by rarefaction from iNEXT
  dplyr::filter(Method == "Rarefaction") %>%
  # Now, let's draw the plot, be sure to group by the samples if using geom_line!
  ggplot(aes(x = m, y= qD, color = Subtype, group = SampleID)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  # Facet with the station to see the samples better 
  facet_grid(Order.q~Subtype, scales = "free") + 
  # scale_color_manual(values = Subtype_Color) + 
  labs(x = "Number of Sequences (Library Size)", 
       y = "Effective Number of ASVs") + 
  theme_bw() + 
  #guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, vjust = 1, hjust = 1),
        legend.title = element_blank()) 
```


While the rarefaction curves from `ggiNEXT` agglomerated the data together, it was hard to see individual samples. Above, we can start to tease apart specific samples within each station that appear higher. 

**Some initial take-aways:**  

- *Richness:*  
    - There appears to be a difference between the biomes in the total richness.
    - There are potential outlier samples in some of the biomes.  
- *Simpson's Diversity:* 
    - The **Seawater 3-um biome** has a bimodal distribution with (2) samples that tend to have more dominant taxa/higher diversity with 370 - 400 dominant species versus (2) samples that have lower diversity around ~150 dominant taxa).
    - **Seawater 0.2-um biome** appears to have the lowest Simpson's diversity as the plateau is mostly all below ~50 dominant taxa.  
    - There is one sample in the **Seawater 3-um biome** that has a much larger Simpson Diversity value compared to other samples. I wonder who those are! 
- *Shannon Diversity:*
    - Here, the trends that were starting to be witnessed in the Shannon diversity are much more amplified!
    
However, all of these changes are qualitative... let's actually quantify by running some stats!

## Richness - Statistical Testing

```{r richness-stats}
# Make a richness data frame
df_richness_POC_Opu <- 
  obs_div_df %>%
  subset(., Host %in% c("POC")
         & ! Transplant %in% c("Genotype2")
         & Site %in% ("Opunohu")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(Method == "Observed") %>%
  dplyr::filter(Order.q == 0)

# Add the statistical test! 
kruskal.test(qD ~ station_names, data = richness_df)

library(ordinal)
library(emmeans)

# 1. Fit your Cumulative Link Mixed Model (as done previously)
fit_clmm <- clmm(factor(qD) ~ FullTreatment + (1 | Individual), data = df_richness_POC_Opu)

# 2. Obtain estimated marginal means on the latent/log-odds scale
clmm_emmeans <- emmeans(fit_clmm, ~ FullTreatment)

# 3. Perform pairwise post-hoc tests (using Holm adjustment for multiple tests)
clmm_pairs <- pairs(clmm_emmeans, adjust = "holm")

# View the contrast results (Z-tests and adjusted p-values)
print(clmm_pairs)

# 4. Transform results to Odds Ratios (highly recommended for interpretation)
# This shows the relative odds of scoring higher vs. lower between time points
summary(clmm_pairs, type = "response")

# friedman.test(qD ~ FullTreatment | Individual, data = df_richness_POC_Opu)
# 
# library(ARTool)
# library(lme4)
# 
# # Fit the aligned rank transform model
# m <- art(qD ~ factor(FullTreatment) + (1 | Individual), data = richness_df)
# 
# # Run ANOVA on the transformed data
# anova(m)
# 
# # 1. Post-hoc for a specific main effect (e.g., 'time')
# art.con(m, "FullTreatment", adjust = "holm")
# 
# # 2. Post-hoc for an interaction effect (e.g., 'treatment' across 'time')
# art.con(m, ~ treatment * time, adjust = "holm")

# 
my_comparisons <- list( c("Copano\nWest", "Copano\nEast"), c("Copano\nWest", "Mesquite\nBay"), 
                        c("Copano\nWest", "Aransas\nBay"), c("Copano\nWest", "Shipping\nChannel"),
                        c("Copano\nEast", "Mesquite\nBay"), c("Copano\nEast", "Aransas\nBay"),
                        c("Copano\nEast", "Shipping\nChannel"), c("Mesquite\nBay", "Aransas\nBay"),
                        c("Mesquite\nBay", "Shipping\nChannel"), c("Aransas\nBay", "Shipping\nChannel"))

# Now, plot it!
richness_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = station_names, y = qD, fill = station, color = station)) + 
  geom_jitter(size = 2.5) + 
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = station_colors) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = station_colors) + 
  labs(y = "Effective Number of ASVs") + 
  # Add pairwise comparisons p-value
  stat_compare_means(comparisons = my_comparisons,
                     tip.length = 0, hide.ns = TRUE) + 
  stat_compare_means(label.y = 50)  +   # Add global p-value
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        legend.title = element_blank())
```

# Diversity vs Salinity 

## Salinity - what is it? 

PSU  = practical salinity unit 

- 1 PSU = 1 g of salt per 1,000 grams of water
- 1 PSU = 1 ppt (part per thousand)

The gradient is: 

- Freshwater = 0-0.5
- Brackish = 0.5 - 30
- Marine = >30

```{r div-vs-salinity, fig.height=3.5, fig.width=6, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# How does biodiversity change over the salinity gradient
iNEXT_manual_df %>%
  dplyr::filter(Method == "Observed") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = salinity_psu, y = qD)) + 
  facet_wrap(.~Order.q, scales = "free") + 
  geom_point(aes(color = station)) + 
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~poly(x, 2)) + 
  labs(x = "Salinity (PSU)", y = "# of ASVs") + 
  scale_color_manual(values = station_colors) + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.title = element_blank()) 
```


Here, there appears to be a few different results: 

- There appears to be a negative & linear relationship between salinity and Richness. This indicates that freshwaters have the highest number of ASVs (genearlly around ~150 ASVs) and as we gain more and more salt in the water, there are fewer species (closer to ~110 ASVs)! We will test this more below. :)  
- Taking the Richness relationship above, we also need to note that there seems to be a high amount of variability within the brackish samples, 
- Shannon & Simpson diversity appear to have a "U" shaped diversity curve!  
- The "U" shape indicates that diversity measures that also weight relative abundance (common and dominant taxa) is highest at the two ends of the spectrum... this indicates that there are fewer dominant species in brackish waters.  

### Explore Richness More

```{r richness-vs-salinity, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# Make a richness data frame
richness_df <- 
  obs_div_df %>%
  dplyr::filter(Method == "Observed") %>%
  dplyr::filter(Order.q == 0)

# Actually run the linear model
rich_vs_sal_lm <- 
  lm(qD ~ salinity_psu, data = richness_df)

# Show me the model results
rich_vs_sal_lm

# Type?
class(rich_vs_sal_lm)

# Summary of lm
summary(rich_vs_sal_lm)
```

In the output:

- **Coefficients** refer to the 𝛽’s
- **Estimate** is the estimate of each coefficient
- **Std. Error** is the standard error of the estimate
- **t value** is the coefficient divided by its standard error
- **Pr(>|t|)** is the p-value for the coefficient
- The **residual standard error** is the estimate of the variance of 𝜖
- **Degrees of freedom** is the sample size minus # of coefficients estimated
- **R-squared** is (roughly) the proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the model, instead we should always report the **adjusted R-squared**, which takes into penalizes the addition of unnecessary predictors, which provides a more accurate measure of model fit.
    - Note that the R-squared value will always increase/stay the same when you add more predictors, even if they are not relevant!
- The **F-statistic** compares the fit of the model as a whole to the null model (with no covariates)
    - When comparing models, we always want to take the model with the higher F-statistic because it indicates a stronger relationship between the predictor varaibles and the dependent variables, suggesting that the model is better. 


```{r plot-richness-sal, fig.height=4, fig.width=4, warning = FALSE, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE}
richness_df %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = salinity_psu, y = qD)) + 
  geom_point(aes(color = station)) + 
  stat_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  labs(x = "Salinity (PSU)", y = "# of ASVs") + 
  scale_color_manual(values = station_colors) + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.title = element_blank()) + 
  geom_label(aes(x = 20, y = 70), hjust = 0, 
             label = paste("Adj R2 = ",signif(summary(rich_vs_sal_lm)$adj.r.squared, 2),
                           "\nIntercept =",signif(rich_vs_sal_lm$coef[[1]],3),
                           " \nSlope =",signif(rich_vs_sal_lm$coef[[2]], 2),
                           " \nP =",signif(summary(rich_vs_sal_lm)$coef[2,4], 2)))
```
